output.headline: Serbia’s student movement sweeps to power as Vučić concedes defeat
output.bodyHtml:
The long-serving leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vučić, has conceded defeat, ushering in a seismic political shift after a historic election that saw ​the increasingly authoritarian leader pitted against a student-led movement that had spent two years protesting against his government.

Vučić pointed to preliminary results that suggested voters had overwhelmingly backed the students, potentially giving them a majority in the country’s 250-seat parliament.

“We still do not have final ⁠results,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade. “On the basis of a sample … it is clear ⁠that we have lost these ​elections, the Student ‌List has ‌won, they will have between 135 ‌and 140 seats and we will have 105.”

A representative sample by the ​CeSID-IPSPS pollsters suggested that the ​Student List’s candidate list will have ​138 deputies, while Vučić’s rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) garnered 104 seats. The remaining seats ‌were likely to be shared ​between ethnic ​national minority parties, said the pollsters.

As news broke that Vučić’s 12 years in power had come to an end, celebrations erupted on the streets of Belgrade and other cities.

In the capital, Ivana, 43, was ecstatic. “This feels like New Year’s Eve to me, like three New Year’s Eves all at once, really,” she said. “We can finally breathe again.” She added that she was hoping for swift accountability for top members of the ousted regime, a key campaign pledge from the Student List.

Others offered handshakes, high fives and hugs to police officers in the streets, while a chorus of honking horns rang out from passing cars.

At the headquarters of the Student List, supporters chanted “Victory, victory!” as they applauded, cried and traded hugs. “Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Saičić, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”

The scenes of joy came hours after a record number of voters turned up to cast their ballot on Sunday. Across the country, long lines snaked out of polling stations, with some reporting wait times of up to two hours. By 7pm local time pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put the turnout at 67.6%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.

The high turnout, along with the estimated 150,000 people who flocked to the students’ final pre-election rally last week in Belgrade, fuelled early speculation that the students may have rallied enough support to launch a new political era in the Balkan country.

In the lead-up to the vote, opinion polls had varied wildly, with analysts pointing to the high degree of uncertainty at play as the candidates representing the grassroots student movement went up against Vučić’s SNS.

The results were watched across the world as part of 10 pivotal days of elections across the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. The victory for the student-led movement in Serbia is also likely to reverberate across Europe, adding momentum to the youth and student protests that have rocked cities across the continent.

As people waited for the election results to come in, speculation had begun to swirl online about whether Vučić would seek to hold on to power regardless. His swift admission of defeat, however, was reminiscent of his ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, fuelling hopes of a democratic resurgence to central Europe.

The high-stakes election in the EU-candidate country traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed at the Novi Sad railway station, killing 16 people. The tragedy set off protests among students, snowballing into a broad anti-government movement as evidence suggested that slipshod construction, fraud and corruption were to blame for the roof collapse.

As Vučić, the increasingly authoritarian leader who has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, grappled with mounting pressure from the students, he resigned the presidency last month to gamble on snap elections.

The students seized on the chance to transform the movement into political power. They announced a slate of 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, ranging from academics to athletes and farmers, as they called on voters to back their push to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy.

The campaign pitted them against the political monolith of Vučić’s SNS party, leaving them in an uphill battle against a ruling party that had taken over almost all of the broadcast channels and which wielded ministries and other state institutions as political tools.

Vučić had repeatedly sought to undermine the students by accusing them of being stooges of foreign powers, a charge that the students have dismissed. As he pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, Vučić sought to present himself as a leader capable of walking the diplomatic tightrope between the country’s ties with the west, and Russia and China to steer Serbia through global uncertainties.

Undaunted, the students took to the streets, staging rallies, turning up in the rural areas that had long been Vučić strongholds and going door-to-door as they sought to pitch themselves as the anti-establishment candidates and to rally voters behind their slogan of “Serbia or Mafia?”

The message was reiterated on Sunday as Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate on the Student List and the Euroleague Basketball president, cast his ballot in Belgrade.

“Today, above all, Serbia is fighting for freedom and for the return of a country that has been hijacked,” Bodiroga told reporters. “Serbia is voting today to decide which direction it will take – towards the future or the past.”

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, both international and local election monitors expressed concerns about detentions and reports of surveillance and cyber-attacks against activists.

On Sunday, independent monitoring groups warned of recorded cases of photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters, attempted vote-buying and carousel voting.

Among them was Raša Nedeljkov of the election monitory CRTA, who said that “a large number of irregularities continue to be recorded, while violent incidents outside polling stations are also becoming increasingly frequent”.
output.standfirst: Record turnout of 67.6% carried the Student List – born from protests over the Novi Sad roof collapse that killed 16 people – to a commanding win over Vučić’s SNS after 12 years in power.
output.progress: Student List candidates, set to take around 138 of parliament's 250 seats, campaigned on a pledge to pursue accountability for the ousted government.

output.headline: Burnham makes the case for reopening Britain's free movement debate with EU
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers but risked a rift with “red wall” Labour MPs, who say it could jeopardise Brexit-voting seats.

The prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.

Burnham also revealed his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in their manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.

The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].

“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

His remarks were supported by Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, as well as Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe. However, Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those Labour MPs who have previously been more cautious about closer ties with Europe, while a number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.

Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she would “like to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be, and then put that to the people at a general election”, and Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means”.

A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion include Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary.

At a New Statesman event during the Labour party conference in September, however, Mahmood said rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.

One senior minister under Keir Starmer said the reopening of the debate on free movement was “brave” given how divisive it had been in the Brexit years. “It’s a question of timing. Public opinion is of a place where you can start to have this debate,” he said. “Theresa May, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer: what they were all trying to do was get as close as possible without freedom of movement. There is now the a possibility of being brave and making the case on single market and free movement without going for rejoin.”

Labour MPs with pro-Brexit seats have expressed scepticism about rejoining the bloc, including Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.

One red wall MP said they thought debating free movement was the right thing to do but many colleagues in the north-east, especially in coastal areas, had begun to raise serious concerns. “These MPs are definitely raising the alarm,” they said. “Andy may have to work out if he can win without them, which is brutal but true.” Another Labour MP from a Brexit-voting area said it would “undoubtedly put seats at risk to Reform” but that Burnham was making an argument from a position of strength, having taken the party to higher poll ratings in recent weeks.

Worries were brought up publicly on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “1 million young people that are out of work”.

In his party conference speech last month, Burnham fired the starting gun on the argument about rejoining the EU as one potential route, but his latest comments suggest he appears to be favouring the option that would avoid a referendum.

Although Labour’s manifesto pledges no return to free movement and the single market, Burnham signalled it could still be up for discussion at next month’s EU summit.

Burnham’s comments at the weekend drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”.

“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.

Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move more freely for jobs within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.

Luke Tryl, a polling and focus groups expert at the More in Common thinktank, said on Sunday that people tended to be less concerned about free movement given years of high non-EU migration but would be more exercised about EU budget contributions or joining the euro.

During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote.

Burnham’s decision to open the debate on free movement was welcomed by some businesses, which have grown frustrated at the lack of progress on the issue, and on reducing the extra paperwork required to do business with EU customers since Brexit – both seen as obstacles to faster economic growth.

The British Chambers of Commerce lobby group called for the Treasury to analyse the various economic options for different forms of EU-UK relationships. Most economic studies have concluded that a closer EU relationship would benefit the UK economy.

William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said the common understanding strategy agreed by Keir Starmer in May 2025 was “approaching the ceiling of what can be achieved”.

This week’s budget is expected to underscore the damage to the economy from Brexit, including from a drop in net migration. The Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said that if migration falls by 300,000 over the next five years it would translate to a hit to government tax revenues of £4.7bn in 2029-30, reducing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies, another thinktank, estimated that lower net migration estimates would reduce the chancellor’s “headroom” by between £1bn and £5bn by 2031-32, depending on how the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) chooses to model the expected reductions in population.

The OBR has previously estimated that Brexit barriers to trade and free movement have caused a long-term hit of about 4% of UK output.
output.standfirst: His call for an honest debate on EU ties is backed by cabinet colleagues and business leaders seeking economic growth, but risks a split with red wall Labour MPs, who say it could cost seats to Reform.
output.progress: The British Chambers of Commerce has urged the Treasury to analyse the economic case for closer EU ties.

output.headline: Engineers work to restore power as Storm Boelo disruption continues
output.bodyHtml:
Scotland's government convened an emergency "resilience room" and engineers worked to reconnect hundreds of thousands of homes to the power network, as Storm Boelo continued to batter the UK. Two people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power by the storm.

Two men, one aged 60 and the other in his 20s, were killed by falling trees on Sunday, police said. The 60-year-old died in south-west Scotland while the man in his 20s was killed in London.

A spokesperson for Police Scotland said: “We were made aware of a 60-year-old man having been struck by a falling tree on a minor road at Mid Kelton at about 10.30am on Sunday, 25 October 2026.

“The man was pronounced dead at the scene. There are no suspicious circumstances and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal in due course.”

In London, the man was killed when a tree fell on to his car at 12.40pm as he drove through Mill Hill in the north of the city.

Ch Insp Guy Ellwood said: “Our thoughts are with the loved ones of the young man who lost his life.”

The Scottish government's resilience room met on Sunday afternoon to discuss the storm's impact, with ministers focusing on the outages and how they were being restored. Scotland's first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency agencies and forecasters to discuss the government's response, amid warnings that similar conditions would return early next week.

Engineers had restored power to 344,900 customers but 82,600 remained disconnected, the ENA said on Sunday morning. The figure included more than 30,000 homes across Scotland.

The ENA said: “The networks have been focused on reconnecting customers this morning, though the continuing severe weather in some regions is limiting network engineers’ opportunities to safely start the work of restoring customers’ power today and access to certain areas remains difficult. Engineers are working around the clock to identify and fix faults.”

By 5pm on Sunday, approximately 53,000 homes in Scotland were still without power, according to updates from SP Energy Networks and Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks.

Across Great Britain, 161,400 customers were without power at that point, according to the Energy Networks Association (ENA).

The adverse weather that arrived in northern parts of the UK on Saturday evening was the second named storm in as many days, after Storm Austen brought strong winds to south-west England on Friday.

The Met Office said wind speeds widely reached 60-70mph, affecting areas in an amber warning zone that came into force at 9pm on Saturday.

The warning covered Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, with gusts reaching more than 80mph in exposed coastal spots.

The island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides was hit by 82mph winds, according to the forecaster, while wind speeds reached 84mph in Argyll and Bute and 83mph in Snowdonia (Eryri).

Train travel was disrupted on Sunday. Network Rail Scotland shared an image of flooding from the tracks to the platform at one Glasgow station, and fallen trees above the lines near another. Speed restrictions were in place across Scotland and several sections of its railways were closed, the operator added.

Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, and it reminded people living near rail lines to firmly secure objects in their gardens.

Some flights were diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford airport and others were cancelled.

The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items in gardens and to stay indoors as the storm posed a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.

The Met Office chief forecaster, Jason Kelly, said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.

“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts. People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”

Several events were cancelled this weekend due to the inclement weather. Visit Liverpool said the River of Light event, featuring illuminated artworks, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”, while London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations on Sunday were cancelled on the advice of independent health and safety experts.

Edinburgh Castle was closed on Sunday because of the high winds and adverse weather, while the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire was also closed for the day, after its Fountains by Floodlight event on Saturday evening was cancelled.

The Environment Agency had issued six warnings as of 1.45pm that flooding was expected for spots in northern parts of England, as well as 50 alerts stating flooding was possible. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency said 17 flood warnings and 11 flooding alerts were active as of the same time.

Cumbria police said they had received a number of calls overnight to localised flooding and fallen trees blocking roads across the county, and urged motorists to drive with care while emergency services worked to clear the obstructions.

The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings, which cover parts of England farther south, as well as north Wales and the whole of Northern Ireland.

Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday, bringing 76mph winds to St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph recorded at Aberporth in south Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.

Stuart Wilson, from Transport Scotland, said “significant recovery work” was required before the network returned to normal.

The Scottish social justice and housing secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, said on Sunday: “Disruption to travel is likely to continue into tomorrow and I strongly recommend people check official sources such as the Met Office, Traffic Scotland, transport operators and local authority channels before setting out.

“While we expect some respite from the adverse weather during the day on Monday, there is a possibility of more severe weather conditions early on in the week and we urge everyone to continue to follow advice and heed any warnings.”
output.standfirst: Engineers are working around the clock to reconnect homes and Scotland's government convened its emergency response, as Storm Boelo killed two men and left 160,000 properties without power, with more severe weather forecast early this week.
output.progress: Engineers are working around the clock to fix faults and reconnect customers, and Scotland's government convened emergency talks with agencies and forecasters on the response.

output.headline: Burnham doubles rough sleeping funding to almost £900m ahead of Christmas target
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham is to double spending on ending rough sleeping to almost £900m by the end of the current parliament, as he steps up efforts to get people off the streets by Christmas.

The prime minister has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.

As he prepared for a Downing Street summit on ending rough sleeping on Monday, Burnham said the budget would bring a further £432m commitment to helping to tackle homelessness.

The sum is on top of an initial £442m from Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government budgets that will be allocated to the problem before March 2027.

Speaking ahead of the meeting, which will bring together charities and businesses, Burnham said: “Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t.

“Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament too.

“But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we’re bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts.”

Related: Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by Christmas

Burnham’s mission to end rough sleeping is already under way with just two months to go before his deadline. There are specialist outreach teams and new accommodation spaces operating in Coventry, and further provision is being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden over the coming weeks.

The additional funding is being provided in an attempt to solve the problem of rough sleeping in the longer term. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.

Burnham has previously said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support and, understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.

He has said ending rough sleeping across the country will only be possible “if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve”.

The prime minister’s rough sleeping summit on Monday will bring together businesses, charities, housing providers and local leaders as they attempt to create more lasting changes.

Alongside the government, other organisations are making pledges towards solving the problem, with the National Housing Federation working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.

Virgin Media O2 will provide practical digital support to frontline organisations, while the charities St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless will work with L’Oréal on hair salons and wellbeing provision for those who have been sleeping rough.

Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said it was a “big ambition” and the government would “not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas”.

She said: “The first step is giving people a roof over their head and freedom from the nightly struggle to find somewhere safe to sleep. But Christmas is only the beginning and that’s why we will keep working together to tackle the root causes of homelessness and end rough sleeping for good.”

The homelessness charity Shelter welcomed the announcement. Its acting CEO, Mairi MacRae, said the funding showed “the government understands that a safe home is not a privilege, it is a necessity”.

However, the Conservatives dismissed the move, with Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, accusing the government of wanting to spend too much money on ending rough sleeping.

Related: Why are rough sleepers dying a stone’s throw from luxury waterfront houses in Victoria?

“Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester,” she said. “Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.”

Referring to the chancellor, Lam said: “[John] Healey must use his budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices. Instead of piling more costs on to hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.”
output.standfirst: Burnham will add £432m in this week's budget, taking total funding to tackle rough sleeping to almost £900m as charities, housing providers and businesses join the push; the Conservatives dismissed the plan as empty promises.
output.progress: Downing Street is bringing together charities, housing associations and businesses, including the National Housing Federation and L'Oréal, to find homes and support for rough sleepers.

output.headline: French unions rally to defend the right to protest
output.bodyHtml:
Trade unions and France's Human Rights League are urging the government to abandon a bill that would make protesters liable for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves. In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France's Human Rights League wrote: "This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law."

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades. Emmanuel Macron, the French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.

Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.

The senate will this week debate the government's proposed "vandals pay" law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.

Related: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing

Lecornu said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain's victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was "absolutely essential" after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.

The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring's presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.

Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France's highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to "bring back order to France".

The RN has claimed the "vandals pay" bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: "Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying." She said: "We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?"

Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon's radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the "vandals pay" law "would mean the end of street demonstrations" in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: "No demonstration could take place again in our country."

At this weekend's protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed "illegitimate" and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.

Related: NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game

At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage.

Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: "Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties." He said this was "unprecedented" and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.
output.standfirst: Trade unions and France's Human Rights League are urging the government to scrap a 'vandals pay' bill making protesters liable for up to €10,000 in damage caused by others, as the PM meets student demonstrators.
output.progress: Trade unions and France's Human Rights League have urged the bill be scrapped, and the PM meets student protesters on Monday.

output.headline: China widens corruption investigations into more than a million people
output.bodyHtml:
China's disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people last year, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level. When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party, and more than a decade later the pace of investigations has not slowed.

The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders. In January, Zhang Youxia, China's top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military's top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC).

A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC's head of discipline. Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.

As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. The "fifth plenum" began on Monday and is set to focus on "major issues on advancing the party's full and rigorous self-governance", according to Chinese state media. In party-speak, "governance" is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.

Related: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes

The plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party's energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP's Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy. The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year's 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.

But for those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions. As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.

Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, explained that in Xi's worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. "If you're corrupt, you're not politically loyal. If you're politically loyal, you're not corrupt," Brown said. He added that in the CCP system, "corruption is not just material things", but also "spiritual corruption", which includes political disloyalty.

Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: "Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party's.

"Xi's answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done," Thomas said.

Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party's credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. "It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi's] worldview," said Brown. "Everyone else is corrupt".

In the past, Xi has warned that the party could "lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history" if it could not get its house in order. "This is by no means an exaggeration," he said.

Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi's political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.

Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are "the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline".
output.standfirst: China's disciplinary authorities investigated more than a million people last year, as the party's fifth plenum meets amid questions over whether the enduring campaign is about corruption or about loyalty to Xi Jinping.

output.headline: Four-year-old girl dies after fall from tower block in Barking
output.bodyHtml:
A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in east London.

She was injured after “falling from height” at an address in St Paul’s Road, Barking, on Saturday and died in hospital, the Metropolitan police said.

Officers were called on Saturday at 11am. A police spokesperson said: “Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service, where emergency first aid was administered.

“The girl, aged four, was taken to hospital but, very sadly, later died from her injuries. Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child’s family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

“An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious.”

A spokesperson for the London ambulance service said it sent ambulance crews, a clinical team manager, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic practitioner and London’s air ambulance to the scene.

“We treated a child at the scene before taking the patient to a London major trauma centre,” the ambulance spokesperson said.

Anyone with information about the incident has been asked to contact police on 101.
output.standfirst: The Metropolitan police say the incident at an address in St Paul’s Road is not believed to be suspicious, with an investigation into the circumstances now under way

output.headline: Maguire says Manchester United squad are fully behind Carrick
output.bodyHtml:
Harry Maguire, United’s captain in Bruno Fernandes’ absence, insisted that the squad were “fully behind” Michael Carrick. He said: “Coming into the team last season he turned things around and got Champions League football this season.

As individuals, we’re not playing well enough. We have to look at ourselves and find something within ourselves to bring more to the team. That’s every player that I’m talking about. When things aren’t going your way you have to do the basics well.”

Carrick was defiant after the 3-0 humbling, insisting he was not expecting to be removed from his post. “I totally understand the situation,” Carrick said of his job prospects. “I’m not expecting anything in ­particular, to be honest. Carrying on as normal and I love this place.”

Manchester United’s hierarchy are in crisis talks over whether or not to sack Carrick as head coach after he oversaw another torrid defeat, against Bournemouth at Old ­Trafford on Sunday, that left his job in the balance.

Related: Michael Carrick on the brink after Manchester United are humiliated by Bournemouth

But the United executive are actively considering his dismissal, the Guardian understands, with the expectation at the club being that Carrick will be sacked.

Eddie Howe remains the preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox, United’s director of football, should there be a change in the dugout, with the former Newcastle manager’s extensive Premier League experience placing him ahead of other potential targets.

Howe would be less expensive to bring in than Unai Emery, another admired candidate, given that Aston Villa would demand about £20m in compensation for the Spaniard.

Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach, is highly regarded by Christopher Vivell, United’s head of recruitment, but Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls football policy at United. Antonio Conte is another who may be in the frame.

Carrick, who left Bruno Fernandes out of his starting lineup – insisting before kick-off that he did so for football reasons and not because of the captain’s criticism of his tactics after the midweek Champions League defeat at Como – said: “I’ll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club, whatever decision is made on anything really. So that’s kind of it. I’m not expecting anything either way.

“It’s a tough situation, there’s no hiding from it. What it looks like and what’s next I really don’t know. I will always do my best for the football club and I won’t change that now. I love what I do and I feel the responsibility – we’ll have to wait and see.”

United endured a sixth defeat in 12 games in all competitions after Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson scored for Marco Rose’s side. They have won only once in the league this season and sit in 16th. Their last win was on 10 September, against Sabah in the Champions League.

The club cannot announce a sacking until they inform the New York Stock Exchange, which is closed at weekends. When Ruben Amorim was sacked in January, the decision was taken on the Sunday night after the coach’s explosive press conference following a draw at Leeds, but was not announced until the next day.

Carrick made a point of applauding the home supporters at the end of the match, pumping his hand to his chest as he walked past a supportive Stretford End. As soon as he disappeared down the tunnel, boos met Fernandes, who was following the manager, alongside other United players.

“It wasn’t a farewell from me,” Carrick said. “I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.

“To have that connection with the supporters, it’s mixed emotions, it’ll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support. The situation is where we are and we haven’t had results or performances that have been good enough.”

On his decision to omit Fernandes, who was an unused substitute, Carrick said: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference, but those are the decisions we made today.”

• Job in balance after 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth, with the club’s hierarchy expecting to sack him

  • Howe remains director of football Jason Wilcox’s preferred candidate
